subtitle: The June 1970 draft of the first official host-to-host protocol of the early ARPA network, offered for comment.

tldr.problem: Hosts on the early network needed one agreed way to open connections, regulate how much data flows over them, and close them again.
tldr.mechanism: Hosts exchange short control commands (such as STR, RTS, CLS and ALL) on link 1; the receiver tells the sender how much buffer space is available, and the sender never sends more text than that.
tldr.outcome: The authors hoped it would become the initial official protocol, open to criticism until July 13, 1970. It was updated by RFC 57.

today: RFC 54 is a 1970 draft whose status is recorded as Unknown, and it was updated by RFC 57. The text shows an early stage of the host-to-host protocol, not a current specification.

sections.title: A Protocol Offered for Comment
sections.content:
RFC 54, by Steve Crocker, Jon Postel, John Newkirk and Mike Kraley, submits a protocol for criticism and comment, as advertised in NWG/RFC 53. The authors intend it to become the initial official protocol and invite criticism until July 13, 1970. After that date a decision would be made whether to adopt it, or a slight variation, or to redesign it.

It covers only network-wide issues, which the authors define as message formats and restrictions on message content. Writing a Network Control Program (NCP) and choosing system calls are strictly local matters. A prototypical NCP is described in RFC 55.
sections.eli5: The authors are saying: here are our rules, tell us what is wrong with them before we make them official.

sections.title: Connections, Sockets and Links
sections.content:
A connection is a simplex communication path, meant to run between two processes. The protocol provides for establishing connections, regulating flow over them, and terminating them, plus ancillary functions such as simulated interrupt pulses and echo tests.

Connections are named by a pair of sockets. Sockets are polarized: even-numbered ones are receive sockets and odd-numbered ones are send sockets, and one of each is needed. Each connection is also assigned a unique link, chosen by the receiver. Link 1 between each pair of hosts is the control link, link zero is reserved for intra-network use, links 32 to 255 are reserved for experiment and expansion, and so only links 2 through 31 are for regular use.

The text describes sockets as 40 bit names in the discussion, while the command formats give my socket and your socket as 32 bit fields made of a 24 bit user number and an 8 bit AEN.
sections.eli5: A connection is a one-way pipe. Each end has a numbered socket, and a lane number called a link keeps its traffic separate from the others.

sections.title: Flow Control with Allocations
sections.content:
The one substantive change from the already agreed protocol is a new flow control scheme. The receiving host allocates buffer space for each connection and tells the sender how much space, in bits, is available. The sender keeps a counter per connection, starts it at zero, raises it by control commands from the receiver, and lowers it by the text length of each message sent. It may not send text longer than the counter, so the counter never goes below zero.

The command ALL <link> <space> carries the allocation and is sent only from receiver to sender. The RFC admits an obvious limitation: the receiver cannot rely on average buffer usage, since the worst case is always assumed. Adaptive allocation is said to be feasible but is left for later. Separately, a sender is held by the local IMP from sending another message on a connection until the RFNM for the previous message arrives.
sections.eli5: The listener says how many boxes it has room for, and the speaker only sends that many, waiting for more room before sending more.

sections.title: Control Commands
sections.content:
A regular message has a 32 bit leader, marking, text and padding. A regular message on link 1 is a control message, and its text is a whole number of control commands. Every command code is 8 bits.

To open a connection, the prospective sender sends STR and the prospective receiver sends RTS, which also carries the link. A matching pair, where each side's my socket equals the other's your socket, establishes the connection. CLS closes it, and each side must send and receive one before the sockets are free again. INR and INS carry interrupts, ECO and ERP are a simple echo test, NOP does nothing, and ERR reports an apparent error. The text defines no specific errors, and says hosts should log them.
sections.eli5: Each command is a short note with a number: one says 'let us talk', one says 'I am done', one says 'you may send this much more'.
